title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation
authors: Ximo Zhu, Ruiqi Liu, Yi Han, Zhengan Wu, Gengsheng Li, ZiAn Wang
abstract: Proprietary language models exhibit strong reasoning and coding capabilities, but their output distributions are inaccessible, making fine-grained distillation methods that rely on teacher logits difficult to apply directly to black-box models. We observe that rich textual feedback from a black-box teacher can be treated as privileged information (PI) and converted, through a PI-conditioned privileged teacher, into dense supervision signals on the student's own trajectories. However, what PI should be acquired from the teacher to most effectively support student learning remains unclear. PI strategies that differ in where they focus, what information they request, and how much detail they provide can have substantially different effects on the current student, and their relative effectiveness can further change as training progresses. Based on this observation, we propose Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation (EvoOPD), which treats PI acquisition itself as an optimization problem and maintains a PI Strategy Bank that evolves with the student state. EvoOPD uses the measured repair utility of PI on the current student to adapt the focus, information type, and granularity of teacher feedback, allowing the acquired information to continually match the student's learning needs. We systematically evaluate EvoOPD on mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students. EvoOPD achieves the best overall performance in all six model-task settings, improving over the strongest baseline in each setting by an average of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 points in code. Further analysis shows that the relative effectiveness of PI acquisition strategies changes with student state, making a fixed strategy difficult to sustain as the best choice throughout distillation.

infographic.key_insight: EvoOPD improves black-box distillation by evolving teacher-feedback strategies to match the student's changing learning needs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach enables dense supervision from proprietary models without accessing their logits, using textual feedback and a privileged-information-conditioned teacher.
method: Acquire textual feedback as privileged information on student-generated trajectories.
Convert that feedback into dense supervision through a privileged-information-conditioned teacher.
Evolve a strategy bank using measured repair utility to adapt feedback focus, type, and detail.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across mathematical reasoning and code generation with Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B students, EvoOPD leads all six model-task settings, averaging gains of 2.14 percentage points in mathematics and 1.30 in code over each setting's strongest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Adaptive strategy evaluation and feedback acquisition may add teacher-query and training overhead; the abstract does not quantify these costs.
infographic.paper_title: EvoOPD: Evolving Privileged Information Strategies for Black-Box On-Policy Distillation

title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning
authors: Lianmin Chen, Junbin Qiu, Chenxing Wei, Yao Shu, Kun He
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization has emerged as a promising approach for memory-efficient large language model (LLM) post-training, yet its reliability in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) remains largely unexplored. Motivated by the distinct data regimes of on-policy RL and fixed-data optimization, we develop a generic variance-theoretic framework to investigate what limits the reliability of ZO gradient estimation. Our analysis reveals that estimation reliability is structurally determined by whether the two finite-difference evaluations are performed on matched data. On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) under the mismatched-data regime produces a $1/μ^2$ oracle-noise amplification that sets an irreducible noise floor as the perturbation scale $μ$ decreases, whereas Boltzmann Targeted SFT (BOLT) under the matched-data regime eliminates this amplification via noise cancellation. We further derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants that cleanly separate the two regimes. These results motivate the ZO-BOLT algorithm, which builds on BOLT's matched-data advantage for reliable ZO optimization of an RLVR-aligned objective. Controlled perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched end-to-end comparisons validate the predicted effect of data matching. Experiments across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks further show that ZO-BOLT consistently improves over the pretrained baseline while retaining a near-inference memory footprint. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/lianmin-chen/the_cost_of_mismatch.

infographic.key_insight: Matching data across the two zeroth-order finite-difference evaluations cancels oracle-noise amplification, whereas mismatched on-policy evaluations amplify it by 1/μ².
infographic.engineering_relevance: ZO-BOLT offers a path to more reliable, memory-efficient LLM post-training by pairing matched-data optimization with an RLVR-aligned objective.
method: Analyze gradient-estimator variance under matched versus mismatched data.
Derive convergence guarantees with explicit constants separating the two regimes.
Build ZO-BOLT on Boltzmann Targeted SFT’s matched-data advantage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Perturbation-scale sweeps and matched-versus-mismatched comparisons support the predicted effect; tests across three models and two mathematical reasoning benchmarks show consistent gains over pretrained baselines with near-inference memory use.
infographic.watch_item: Matched-data cancellation removes the identified amplification mechanism, not all estimation noise; broader task generalization is not established by the reported math benchmarks.
infographic.paper_title: The Cost of Mismatch: Noise Amplification in Zeroth-Order Reinforcement Learning

title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation
authors: Yichen Wang, Yufa Zhou, Siqi Zhu, Haozheng Luo, Jingzhi Bao, Zhichao Liu
abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) extends on-policy distillation (OPD) to consolidate capabilities from multiple teachers. Although prior work reports near-perfect in-distribution (IND) distillation performance, we find that this can mask incomplete capability consolidation beyond the supervised distribution. A preliminary study on synthetic reasoning shows that OPD does not fully transfer teachers' generalization capabilities. We then extend this investigation to real-world tasks, evaluating extrapolative and compositional generalization across mathematical reasoning, coding, agent, and long-context capabilities using Qwen3 models. Across extrapolative settings, OPD and MOPD reach 96.04-102.73% of their teachers' IND scores. Yet their out-of-distribution (OOD) scores remain 2.45-16.25% below the base model's. Across three compositional settings, MOPD improves IND performance over the base model, but its performance on composed tasks as OOD remains 18.19-24.34% below that of the best teachers. To understand these gaps, we examine teacher capability and data coverage as two potential bottlenecks. Jointly alleviating these bottlenecks eliminates OOD forgetting in our experiments and suggests the potential for generalization beyond the teacher. (M)OPD also reduces OOD forgetting on average relative to its reinforcement learning (RL) baselines. Analysis of the associated update geometry reveals smaller and more spectrally concentrated updates on average than those of the RL baselines, along with greater shared update structure under MOPD. Motivated by these findings, we propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve OOD performance while largely preserving IND performance. Our findings identify a blind spot in capability consolidation via (M)OPD, highlighting the need for algorithms that explicitly support OOD retention and generalization.

infographic.key_insight: Near-teacher in-distribution performance after on-policy distillation can mask incomplete transfer of generalization and loss of out-of-distribution capabilities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: When consolidating specialist models, test extrapolative and composed tasks rather than relying on in-distribution scores alone.
method: Evaluate single- and multi-teacher on-policy distillation using synthetic reasoning and Qwen3-based tasks.
Probe teacher capability, data coverage, and update geometry as factors in generalization gaps.
Propose geometry-based patching and base-preserving replay to improve out-of-distribution retention.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across math, coding, agent, and long-context evaluations, extrapolative IND scores reached 96.04–102.73% of teacher scores, while OOD scores were 2.45–16.25% below the base model; composed-task scores were 18.19–24.34% below the best teachers.
infographic.watch_item: Eliminating OOD forgetting by jointly improving teacher capability and data coverage was demonstrated only in the reported experiments, not established as a general guarantee.
infographic.paper_title: On the Generalization Limitation of On-Policy Distillation for Post-RL Consolidation

title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations
authors: Jiaxin Xie, Guowei Dou, Xiang Ji, Wensheng Yu
abstract: Mathematical formalization plays an important role in establishing rigorous and machine-verifiable foundations for mathematical reasoning. With the development of large language models (LLMs) and interactive theorem provers, intelligent agents offer a promising approach to automating the formalization of mathematical theories. This paper presents the Math Foundation Formalization Agent (MFF-Agent), a general-purpose intelligent agent designed to support formalization tasks across multiple mathematical domains. The agent integrates the reasoning capabilities of large language models with the formal verification capabilities of the Rocq proof assistant. It incorporates task classification, tool-assisted execution, verification feedback, and state-based task management to support the generation, refinement, and verification of formal proofs. Unlike an approach focused on a single mathematical theory, the agent is examined through case studies involving Morse--Kelley axiomatic set theory (MK), real numbers, propositional logic, and equivalences of the axiom of choice. These cases investigate its applicability across mathematical foundations and distinguish source-level completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation. The results demonstrate the feasibility of a unified operational framework for heterogeneous foundation-level tasks and clarify the gap between such a framework and a fully integrated mathematical foundation.

infographic.key_insight: MFF-Agent combines LLM reasoning with Rocq verification in a unified workflow for formalizing diverse mathematical foundations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its classify–execute–verify workflow offers a reusable architecture for AI-assisted formalization with tool feedback and explicit task-state tracking.
method: Classify formalization tasks and manage their execution state.
Use LLM reasoning and tools to generate and refine formal proofs.
Use Rocq verification feedback to guide revisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Case studies cover Morse–Kelley set theory, real numbers, propositional logic, and axiom-of-choice equivalences, distinguishing source completion, interactive verification, and reproducible compilation.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports feasibility rather than quantitative performance, and a unified workflow does not establish a fully integrated mathematical foundation.
infographic.paper_title: Math Foundation Formalization Agent: A General-Purpose Approach to Formalizing Mathematical Foundations

title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning
authors: Yangrong Hu, Xueyu Zhou, Yue Wu, Jian Huang
abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is a key component of language model post-training, enabling effective task adaptation and serving as an important foundation for subsequent reinforcement learning. Recent methods seek to improve SFT by introducing token-level weights into the training objective, where these weights are typically derived from a model's output distribution at each token position. To better understand how such weighting schemes affect SFT, we analyze their optimization objectives and theoretically characterize the target distributions they induce. Our analysis shows that dynamic weighting methods, such as Dynamic Fine-Tuning (DFT), induce a heavily sharpened distribution, whereas static weighting methods fit a target distribution proportional to the product of the data distribution and a frozen prior. These findings suggest that static weighting provides a more stable training target, while its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of the prior distribution. Building on this observation, we propose Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT), which uses a frozen copy of the initial model conditioned on privileged information (such as ground truth for mathematical questions) as a prior to provide guidance for token-level weighting during fine-tuning. Through a Bayesian decomposition, we further show that SPFT reweights the standard static prior according to how informative each target token is for predicting the ground-truth outcome, thereby assigning larger weights to more predictive tokens. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that SPFT improves over standard SFT and other baselines across the main settings.

infographic.key_insight: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning (SPFT) uses a frozen initial model with access to privileged information, such as ground-truth answers, to emphasize tokens informative about the correct outcome.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPFT offers a token-weighted fine-tuning approach for mathematical reasoning and code generation, with a stable weighting prior whose quality remains critical.
method: Analyze the target distributions induced by dynamic and static token weighting.
Use a frozen initial model conditioned on privileged information to provide token-level training weights.
Interpret the weights through a Bayesian decomposition that favors outcome-predictive tokens.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improvements over standard SFT and other baselines in mathematical reasoning and code generation, but provides no benchmark names or numerical gains.
infographic.watch_item: Effectiveness depends on the privileged prior's quality, and generating weights requires inference with a frozen model.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Privileged Fine-Tuning

title: Improving Hydrofoil Efficiency Through Simulation-Driven Design Optimization
authors: Ante Sikirica, Ivana Lučin, Marta Alvir, Tin Matulja
abstract: Foil windsurfing is a sport in which competitors fine-tune their setup to optimize performance under varying environmental conditions. However, such adjustments are typically guided by intuition. This paper presents a methodology for improving hydrofoil design using computational fluid dynamics. First, structured light scanning was used to obtain the geometry of a conventional hydrofoil. Subsequently, five derived designs have been explored, inspired by advancements in airplane wing design. Following this, a preliminary design was selected, and a design of experiments approach was implemented. Generated simulation data were used to train a machine learning surrogate, which is ultimately used in the multi-objective design optimization. While the surrogate-based approach yielded promising results, it was limited to exploring a restricted set of design parameters. To overcome this constraint, additional improvements were attained through adjoint optimization, demonstrating that comparable performance can be achieved with a distinctly different hydrofoil design. Finally, the conventional design was refined through adjoint optimization. Notably, adjoint optimization yielded a 15% increase in efficiency. The results suggest that both proposed approaches can produce novel hydrofoil designs capable of outperforming the original configuration under specific conditions; however, due to its inherent flexibility, the adjoint approach with realistic constraints offers more freedom in the design exploration process.

infographic.key_insight: Simulation-driven optimization improved hydrofoil efficiency, with adjoint optimization delivering a reported 15% increase over the conventional design.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CFD-based design optimization can replace intuition-led hydrofoil adjustments with systematic exploration of higher-performing geometries.
method: Capture the conventional hydrofoil geometry using structured light scanning and explore five derived designs.
Train a machine-learning surrogate on design-of-experiments simulation data for multi-objective optimization.
Apply adjoint optimization to refine geometries with greater design freedom.
infographic.evidence_signal: CFD evaluations indicated gains from both optimization approaches, including a 15% efficiency increase from adjoint refinement of the conventional hydrofoil.
infographic.watch_item: Reported gains apply under specific simulated conditions; the abstract does not establish experimental validation or robustness across operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Improving Hydrofoil Efficiency Through Simulation-Driven Design Optimization

title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
authors: Simon Matrenok, Nicolas Menet, Nicolas Flammarion, Andreas Krause
abstract: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.

infographic.key_insight: Repeated-sampling objectives such as pass@k and max@k shift learning pressure toward harder prompts, and their optimal policies can also be obtained with suitably adapted single-sample objectives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: KAPPO lets existing policy optimization methods control sharpening—the loss of behavioral coverage during post-training—without requiring multi-completion training.
method: Derive closed-form optimal policies for KL-regularized pass@k and max@k objectives.
Translate these optima into prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformations for standard @1 objectives.
Apply KAPPO after one-time reference calibration, otherwise retaining the existing training procedure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation report control over sharpening, with single-completion training matching multi-completion @k optimizers at a fraction of the cost.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify calibration overhead, benchmark gains, or compute savings, leaving deployment trade-offs to assess.
infographic.paper_title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training

title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint
authors: Zhenghao Li, Shengbo Wang, Nian Si
abstract: Large language model (LLM) inference, the process by which a pre-trained model receives an input prompt and generates output tokens sequentially, has become increasingly important with the widespread deployment of LLM-based applications. As inference workloads continue to scale, GPU memory has emerged as a critical bottleneck: the long input prompts and generation sequences common in agentic and reasoning workloads lead to substantial key-value (KV) cache usage. In this paper, we study the resulting online scheduling problem from a queueing perspective. Requests arrive stochastically with heterogeneous prompt and output lengths, undergo prefill and autoregressive decode, and compete for a finite KV-cache capacity. Unlike classical queueing models, the duration of a processing step depends on both prefill computation and KV-cache I/O, so service capacity is jointly determined by computation, memory access, and memory occupancy. We develop a fluid model that reduces the system to a multiclass single-server queue with effective service rates capturing computation, memory access, and memory capacity. This fluid analysis yields a $cμ$ priority rule, where the effective service rate $μ$ is jointly determined by computational speed, memory bandwidth, and memory capacity. We prove that this rule minimizes cumulative holding cost in the fluid model and, for a finite workload, also minimizes completion time and maximizes full-run output-token throughput. We then construct a feasible scheduling policy for the original finite system and prove that its scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy. Finally, experiments on a real LLM serving engine using an NVIDIA H800 show that practical implementations of the proposed priority rule substantially reduce average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies.

infographic.key_insight: A cμ priority rule using resource-aware effective service rates is optimal in a fluid model of memory-constrained LLM inference scheduling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLM serving schedulers can reduce latency by prioritizing requests using holding-cost weights and effective service rates that account for compute speed, memory bandwidth, and KV-cache capacity.
method: Reduce stochastic prefill and decode workloads to a multiclass single-server fluid queue.
Prove cμ optimality for cumulative holding cost, plus completion time and full-run output-token throughput for finite workloads.
Construct a feasible finite-system policy whose scaled dynamics converge to the optimal fluid policy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a real LLM serving engine with an NVIDIA H800 report substantially lower average latency while maintaining high throughput relative to existing scheduling policies; the abstract gives no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Optimality is established in the fluid limit, so finite-system performance depends on implementation details and how accurately effective service rates capture resource bottlenecks.
infographic.paper_title: Asymptotic Optimality of $cμ$-Rule for LLM Inference Scheduling under Memory Constraint

title: A Universal Policy Wrapper With Guarantees
authors: Georgiy Malaniya, Anton Bolychev, Pavel Osinenko
abstract: Many control tasks require driving the system into a prescribed goal set and subsequently keeping it there. The considered setting assumes that a working controller is available that provably reaches and maintains the goal, albeit with suboptimal performance. This controller is referred to as the fallback policy. Conversely, although state-of-the-art reinforcement-learning (RL) algorithms can discover policies with impressive empirical performance, the neural networks at their core act as opaque black boxes learned through data-driven exploration and, as such, provide no theoretical mechanism to guarantee that the system will ever reach---and stay within---the prescribed goal set. This article presents CALF-Wrapper, a method that combines the fallback policy with a pretrained RL base policy and uses the critic estimate associated with the base policy to select between them during deployment. The theoretical analysis establishes that CALF-Wrapper inherits the goal-reaching property of the fallback policy under the stated assumptions and provides probability bounds for the settling time and the maximum distance from the goal set over a prescribed time interval. The experimental study evaluates CALF-Wrapper in four simulated control environments of different complexity. Comparisons include the base policy, fallback policy, and constrained reinforcement-learning methods formulated for the same objective. Sensitivity and ablation studies provide direct hyperparameter recommendations. The experiments show how CALF-Wrapper can provide effective task performance while attaining the maximum possible observed goal-reaching rate. CALF-Wrapper requires no additional dynamics model, online learning, or constrained optimization during execution.

infographic.key_insight: CALF-Wrapper combines a pretrained RL policy with a provably goal-reaching fallback controller, inheriting the fallback’s goal-reaching guarantee under stated assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables deployment of performant RL controllers without requiring an additional dynamics model, online learning, or constrained optimization during execution.
method: Start with a pretrained RL policy, its critic estimate, and a certified fallback controller.
Use the critic estimate to select between the RL and fallback policies during deployment.
Establish goal-reaching guarantees and probability bounds on settling time and maximum distance from the goal set.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four simulated control environments, comparisons and ablations show effective task performance with the maximum possible observed goal-reaching rate.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on the stated assumptions and a valid fallback controller; the abstract reports simulation rather than real-world validation.
infographic.paper_title: A Universal Policy Wrapper With Guarantees

title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes
authors: Andrew Gracyk
abstract: We attempt to alleviate failure modes of classical physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) in scenarios of topological pathologies corresponding to punctures, holes, poles, and voids by introducing de Rham cohomological augmentations, or Hodge-de Rham PINNs. Vanilla PINNs often encounter pitfalls in hole-based settings due to discontinuous interfaces, nonzero closed path integration, path dependence, correspondence to exact forms via the exterior derivative, etc., therefore we absolve traditional failures via parameterizing a 1-form by the Hodge-Morrey-Friedrichs (HMF) decomposition for manifolds with boundary, drawing a connection to de Rham cohomology such as through the HMF isomorphism theorem. 1-forms can act as representations of scalar-valued PDE solutions through integral operator mappings. We propose performing a PINN-based loss on the parameterized 1-form through an associated PDE, which subsequently solves the potential-based PINN problem and moreover remedies the failures of vanilla PINNs via the Sobolev-regular operator under a Fréchet differentiation interconnection. The operator relationship often has a nontrivial closed-form and often requires integration or a case-by-case analysis, which we address thoroughly in our experiments. When an integrability condition is not met on our losses, we can equip exhaustion functions to train the networks. We demonstrate our methods on the Aharonov-Bohm effect, which, to our understanding, is largely nonexistent in PINN literature. We develop theoretical guarantees of our methods and demonstrate our pathological safeguards on a broad selection of topologically-adverse problems, including scenarios of inexact forms, and those of nontrivial harmonics and coexact terms.

infographic.key_insight: Hodge–de Rham PINNs represent solutions through decomposed 1-forms to address topological obstructions that can defeat conventional scalar-potential PINNs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could improve physics-informed modeling on domains with holes or singularities where circulation and path dependence matter.
method: Parameterize a 1-form using the Hodge–Morrey–Friedrichs decomposition for manifolds with boundary.
Train with an associated PDE loss and connect the learned form to scalar solutions through integral operators.
Use exhaustion functions when the loss integrability condition is not met.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical guarantees and experiments including the Aharonov–Bohm effect, inexact forms, and nontrivial harmonic and coexact components, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: The operator connecting 1-form and scalar formulations may require problem-specific integration or analysis, complicating implementation.
infographic.paper_title: De Rham cohomological architectures for PINNs and PDEs with topological holes

title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes
authors: Benjamin Jacob Bodner
abstract: The best classical optimizer for a continuous black-box problem depends on its budget and landscape. Existing routers decide from the dimension and budget, past improvement or features fitted to one benchmark, and few test an optimizer's implicit assumptions online. AMM (Adaptive Multi Mode) routes a known budget among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy optimization engines with online probes of curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure. Each probe has a default, a dimension-by-budget validity range and a cost charged to the budget. In its pre-registered development loop on bbob, 32 of 36 predictions held over the last 16 confirmations. AMM was then tested once on held-out bbob instances 101-110 (D=2-40, 10*D-1000*D) against up to seven competitors. It has the highest target share in 382 of 600 function-dimension-budget cells (236 outright, 146 tied) and, by a descriptive posterior rule, is credibly behind in 35, mostly at 10*D and 30*D. At every budget it also leads the controls built from its own engines (the best engine alone, the best engine per dimension and budget, and a greedy schedule), narrowly at 10*D and 30*D, and nevergrad's NgIohTuned. In pre-registered runs its lead over IPOP-CMA-ES holds under affine and box transformations, on box-constrained bbob and, pooled, on rotated f2-f4, but rotating the separable f3 and f4 removes most of the lead there. On held-out MA-BBOB its final share at 2000*D is level with IPOP-CMA-ES's and its anytime area lower. We published AMM as an open-source Python package (pip install amm-optimizer; https://github.com/BjBodner/amm-optimizer).

infographic.key_insight: AMM allocates a fixed evaluation budget across classical optimizers using online landscape probes, achieving the highest target share in 382 of 600 held-out BBOB test cells, including ties.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For continuous black-box engineering problems, AMM offers an open-source Python optimizer that adapts solver choice to landscape structure while charging probe costs to the evaluation budget.
method: Probe curvature, plateaus, separability, kinks, basins and fractal structure online.
Route evaluations among quasi-Newton, trust-region, coordinate, multistart and evolution-strategy engines.
Give each probe a default and a dimension-by-budget validity range.
infographic.evidence_signal: A one-time held-out BBOB evaluation covered instances 101–110, dimensions 2–40 and budgets of 10D–1000D: AMM led outright in 236 of 600 cells, tied for the lead in 146 and was credibly behind in 35 under a descriptive posterior rule.
infographic.watch_item: Advantages were less reliable at tight budgets and under rotated separable landscapes; on held-out MA-BBOB at 2000D, final target share matched IPOP-CMA-ES while anytime area was lower.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Multi Mode: Budget-Aware Routing of Optimizers By Online Landscape Probes

title: Multi-Step Performance Estimation for Gradient Descent under the Polyak Lojasiewicz Condition
authors: Wanli Hong, Shuyang Ling
abstract: Gradient descent is a fundamental algorithm in machine learning and statistical inference. Performance estimation provides a systematic framework for obtaining sharp convergence bounds through semidefinite programming. We study the worst-case performance of constant-stepsize gradient descent over the class of $L$-smooth functions satisfying the $μ$-Polyak--Łojasiewicz (PŁ) inequality. We formulate the $N$-step objective-gap analysis as a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation based on pairwise smoothness constraints and pointwise PŁ inequalities. Since an exact interpolation condition for smooth PŁ functions is not currently available, the resulting SDP provides a valid upper bound on the true worst-case performance. We solve a reduced SDP retaining only consecutive-pair smoothness constraints analytically for every horizon $N$ and every stepsize $t\in(0,2/L)$. The solution exhibits three stepsize regimes. For $0<t\leq 1/L$ and $1/L<t\leq \sqrt{3}/L$, the reduced and full pairwise SDPs have the same optimal value, and the one-step SDP contraction factor tensorizes to a geometric $N$-step rate. For $\sqrt{3}/L<t<2/L$, the reduced-SDP value is nongeometric in the horizon: an initial transient phase is followed by eventual geometric decay. The resulting asymptotic contraction factor is tight for the full pairwise SDP and strictly improves the bound obtained by recursively applying the one-step estimate. Explicit primal and dual feasible solutions certify the results, with numerical SDP experiments guiding their construction. Our results show that analyzing several iterations together can give a better convergence bound than repeatedly applying the sharp one-step SDP bound in the Regime III.

infographic.key_insight: For gradient descent on smooth Polyak–Łojasiewicz functions, multi-step SDP analysis improves on repeated one-step bounds when √3/L < t < 2/L, revealing an initial transient followed by eventual geometric decay.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results sharpen convergence guarantees for constant-step gradient descent under smoothness and Polyak–Łojasiewicz assumptions, especially at larger stable step sizes.
method: Formulate N-step objective-gap bounds as an SDP using pairwise smoothness and pointwise Polyak–Łojasiewicz constraints.
Solve a reduced SDP with consecutive-pair constraints analytically across three step-size regimes.
Certify bounds with explicit primal and dual feasible solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical SDP experiments guided the analytic certificates; the reduced and full SDPs match for 0 < t ≤ √3/L, while the improved asymptotic factor is tight for the full SDP when √3/L < t < 2/L.
infographic.watch_item: These are certified SDP upper bounds, not established exact worst-case rates over smooth Polyak–Łojasiewicz functions, because an exact interpolation condition is unavailable.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Step Performance Estimation for Gradient Descent under the Polyak Lojasiewicz Condition

title: Some algebraic and geometric computations in CH via Chow forms
authors: Robert Andrews, Abhibhav Garg, Rafael Oliveira, Éric Schost
abstract: The problem of decomposing an algebraic variety into more structured components (such as equidimensional, irreducible, or connected components) is a fundamental problem in computer algebra and algebraic geometry. In this work, we study the computational complexity of computing equidimensional components of algebraic varieties, represented via Chow forms. We improve the state-of-the-art complexity bounds from PSPACE to CH, the counting hierarchy, for a number of problems related to equidimensional decomposition, including deciding (1) whether the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety vanishes at a given point, (2) whether a given monomial is in the support of the Chow form of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety, (3) membership in a given equidimensional component of a given algebraic variety, and (4) membership in the closure of the image of an irreducible variety under a polynomial map. As an application of our algorithm to decide membership in the closure of the image of a variety under a polynomial map, we show that the approximate polynomial satisfiability problem can be decided in CH. We also show that the degree of the $k^{\text{th}}$ equidimensional component of a given projective variety can be computed in $\text{FP}^{\text{CH}}$. Our main technical result is the construction of a polylogtime-uniform family of constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits that compute the Chow forms of the equidimensional components of a given projective variety. We construct these circuits by combining the machinery of geometric resolutions together with the uniform constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits of Andrews, Garg, and Schost (FOCS 2026) for the multivariate resultant.

infographic.key_insight: Using Chow forms, the paper improves complexity bounds from PSPACE to the counting hierarchy (CH) for several algebraic-geometry decision problems involving equidimensional components.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These results sharpen theoretical complexity guarantees for symbolic-computation tasks such as component membership and approximate polynomial satisfiability.
method: Represent equidimensional components of projective varieties using Chow forms.
Combine geometric resolutions with threshold circuits for multivariate resultants.
Construct polylogtime-uniform, constant-depth, exponential-size threshold circuits to compute the Chow forms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical complexity results, including CH decision procedures and degree computation in FP^CH, rather than empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The exponential-size circuit construction does not by itself establish a practical or polynomial-time implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Some algebraic and geometric computations in CH via Chow forms

title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents
authors: Xilin Xia
abstract: Dooge asked whether hydrology has laws at the catchment scale. We ask whether a low-dimensional system built under physical laws can match the accuracy of neural networks that outperform process-based models on the same inputs. Three laws constrain a lumped catchment model. Conservation makes it a flux-connected storage network, dissipation fixes the sign of every flux and aggregation determines how the unresolved composition enters the fluxes, through effective laws over threshold distributions and a memory of the forcing. These laws admit four kinds of refinement. A parsimonious model under them, CaRT (11 parameters per catchment), is refined in a loop assisted by AI agents. Each refinement addresses an observed deficit through a hypothesis from the literature. The result, CaRT+, has fourteen states, 35 parameters per catchment and no daily neural network. Most refinements follow from aggregation over thresholds or from variables that carry no water but modulate fluxes. On 602 British and 593 US gauged catchments, single CaRT+ models reach median Nash-Sutcliffe efficiencies of 0.863 and 0.765 in held-out years. A stateful LSTM reaches 0.869 and 0.751 and an entity-aware LSTM 0.862 and 0.754, while three-seed LSTM ensembles remain ahead of the CaRT+ ensemble by 0.003-0.012 in median paired NSE. On 505 drier Australian gauged catchments unused in development, single CaRT+ models reach 0.778 against 0.762 and 0.753 for the two LSTMs. The results suggest that catchment-scale laws exist as laws of form, with the constitutive families shared and only their parameters learned.

infographic.key_insight: A compact, law-constrained catchment model can match or exceed single LSTM models in streamflow prediction without a daily neural network.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Physically structured models offer a competitive alternative to deep learning while retaining explicit water storage and flux relationships.
method: Constrain a storage network using conservation, dissipation and aggregation laws.
Use AI-assisted, literature-grounded refinement to address observed model deficits.
Expand CaRT into CaRT+: 14 states and 35 parameters per catchment.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 602 British, 593 US and 505 Australian catchments, single CaRT+ models achieved median held-out NSEs of 0.863, 0.765 and 0.778; Australian catchments were unused in development.
infographic.watch_item: Three-seed LSTM ensembles retained a 0.003–0.012 median paired NSE advantage over the CaRT+ ensemble in Britain and the US.
infographic.paper_title: From hydrological laws to catchment models: A process-based model matches deep-learning accuracy on three continents

title: Give Up to Get More: Priors, Not Policies, Govern Test-Time Compute Allocation
authors: Jinhyung Bae
abstract: When many inputs share a budget of repeated attempts by a large language model (LLM), a common rule gives harder inputs more. On public math, code and formal-proof samples, the best published difficulty-proportional rule captures half or more of the oracle gain on benchmarks the model mostly solves, but at most 13% on hard workloads, even given true pass rates. Because the value of one more attempt peaks at intermediate difficulty, the optimal static allocation is inverted-U and gives little to inputs that are hopeless at the current budget. In a strict survey of 221 LLM allocation papers, at least 13 give the hardest inputs the most attempts; their easier settings sit at budgets where this is near-optimal, so the cost appears on harder workloads. Acting on it requires knowing which inputs are solvable, so information, not the policy, drives the gain. With a verifier and a prior from a related model's past runs on the same inputs, Thompson Sampling raises the solved share on the hardest workload from 14% to 27%; without such a prior, no policy we tested beats round-robin. For the policies we tested, the gain vanishes between prior rank correlations of about 0.3 and 0.55, which cheap text-based priors barely reach on the weakest models, and it requires a verifier whose false acceptances are rare relative to the pass rate. On new Qwen2.5 samples the pattern holds, and tempering the prior avoids losses on easy workloads. We turn these results into a decision guide.

infographic.key_insight: Reliable priors—not allocation policies alone—drive test-time compute gains, favoring solvable, intermediate-difficulty inputs over the hardest cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For shared retry budgets, prioritize solvability estimates and reliable verification before replacing round-robin with adaptive allocation.
method: Compare difficulty-proportional allocation with an inverted-U static optimum.
Test Thompson Sampling using priors from a related model’s past runs on the same inputs.
Probe sensitivity to prior quality and verifier false acceptances.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across public math, code, and formal-proof samples, difficulty-proportional allocation captures at most 13% of oracle gain on hard workloads; prior-informed Thompson Sampling raises the hardest workload’s solved share from 14% to 27%.
infographic.watch_item: For tested policies, gains vanish around prior rank correlations of 0.3–0.55 and require verifier false acceptances to be rare relative to the pass rate.
infographic.paper_title: Give Up to Get More: Priors, Not Policies, Govern Test-Time Compute Allocation

title: Learning When to Think Aloud in Latent Reasoning
authors: Zhehao Zhou, Tongrui Su, Shengyu Zhu, Da Li, Zeyu Liu, Jun Zhu
abstract: Latent Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves efficiency by shifting intermediate computation into continuous hidden states. However, fully latent methods often struggle on precision-critical tasks such as mathematical reasoning, while existing hybrid approaches retain substantial token-generation overhead. We introduce VITAL, an importance-guided hybrid reasoning framework that selectively verbalizes informative tokens as reasoning anchors while keeping most computation latent. A lightweight gating head dynamically selects between explicit token generation and direct hidden-state feedback. VITAL constructs hybrid trajectories from explicit CoT using token- importance estimation and trains the model through curriculum-based supervised training, followed by reinforcement learning with a reward that balances correctness and conciseness. Experiments show that VITAL consistently out- performs existing fully latent reasoning methods, achieving relative average accuracy gains of 9.6% on GPT-2 and 5.1% on Llama-3.2-1B at comparable reasoning lengths. Compared with hybrid baselines, VITAL achieves higher reasoning accuracy with substantially shorter reasoning trajectories on Qwen3-1.7B.

infographic.key_insight: VITAL selectively verbalizes informative reasoning tokens while keeping most computation latent, improving mathematical reasoning without lengthy explicit chains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive switching between token generation and hidden-state feedback offers a route to more compact mathematical reasoning while preserving precision-critical steps.
method: Estimate token importance in explicit chains of thought to construct hybrid reasoning trajectories.
Use a lightweight gating head to choose explicit token generation or direct hidden-state feedback.
Apply curriculum-based supervised training, then reinforcement learning balancing correctness and conciseness.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports relative average accuracy gains over fully latent methods of 9.6% on GPT-2 and 5.1% on Llama-3.2-1B at comparable reasoning lengths, plus higher accuracy with shorter trajectories than hybrid baselines on Qwen3-1.7B.
infographic.watch_item: Shorter reasoning trajectories do not establish lower end-to-end latency; the abstract provides no wall-clock measurements.
infographic.paper_title: Learning When to Think Aloud in Latent Reasoning

title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry
authors: Bowen Li, Danqing Zhou, Chuan He
abstract: Efficient preconditioning plays an important role in large-scale first-order optimization. In this paper, we propose an adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging ($\text{A}^2$ODA) method for unconstrained convex optimization that adopts low-cost preconditioning based on $p$-norm geometry for $p\in[2,\infty]$. The method is line-search-free and employs a new stepsize selection technique based on an aggregated affine lower model. Its update structure is simple and unified across $p\in[2,\infty]$, with the case $p>2$ requiring no more elaborate updates than the Euclidean case $p=2$. Under a generalized local smoothness condition, we derive a convergence bound that separates the effects of constant and gap-dependent curvature, with the latter potentially yielding faster-decaying terms. In the special case of local smoothness, this bound recovers a nearly optimal convergence rate.

infographic.key_insight: A²ODA combines adaptive acceleration with low-cost p-norm preconditioning for unconstrained convex optimization, using a unified update structure for p ∈ [2, ∞].
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method could simplify geometry-aware first-order solvers by avoiding line searches and keeping updates for p > 2 no more elaborate than the Euclidean case.
method: Use adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging with p-norm preconditioning.
Select step sizes from an aggregated affine lower model without line search.
Separate constant and gap-dependent curvature effects in the convergence analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence bounds, including a nearly optimal rate under local smoothness, but provides no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Practical speedups and sensitivity to the choice of p remain unverified by the abstract's theoretical results.
infographic.paper_title: A simple adaptive accelerated optimistic dual averaging method for unconstrained convex optimization in $p$-norm geometry

title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
authors: Hanzhang Qin, Sophie H. Yu, Yuewei Zhang, Zhi-Hai Zhang
abstract: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

infographic.key_insight: ADP-HT routes LLM calls under a fixed budget by balancing predicted task success against conservative cost estimates to maximize tasks solved before service stops.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Budget-limited LLM services can use spending-aware routing and retry decisions to reduce the risk that costly responses leave later tasks unserved.
method: Learn task-specific success probabilities with a contextual bandit.
Estimate conservative costs from K-bit response-length labels across 2^K quantile intervals.
Adapt the cost penalty to realized spending and budget per remaining task.
infographic.evidence_signal: At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solved over twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline; it led mean cumulative scores at 10 of 14 RouterBench budgets and beat a commercial router’s default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest LiveCodeBench budgets.
infographic.watch_item: Cost-estimate guarantees require calibration, local regularity, and grid coverage; at fixed sample size, increasing K reduces discretization error but increases the estimation allowance.
infographic.paper_title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning

title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models
authors: Antonio Álvarez-López, Jingpu Cheng, Liyan Zhang, Qianxiao Li
abstract: Motivated by the expressive power of neural ordinary differential equations in flow-based generative modeling, we study the approximation of probability measures by pushforwards generated by parameterized families of Lipschitz vector fields. For Wasserstein distances, we establish a quantitative relationship between finite-sample point interpolation and distributional approximation, and derive universality criteria based on $L^p$-approximation of transport maps. In particular, affine-invariant families containing a non-affine vector field are universal from compactly supported absolutely continuous base measures. For total variation, we show that coordinate-wise dynamics are insufficient in dimensions $d\geq 2$ and establish sufficient conditions based on one-dimensional Sobolev approximation and shear-type mixing. We further examine the role of point interpolation, establishing when different regimes relate to one another and when approximate interpolation can be made exact.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-point interpolation and transport-map approximation provide criteria for distributional universality, including Wasserstein universality of affine-invariant vector-field families containing a non-affine field.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results guide the design of expressive neural ODE generators by connecting vector-field capabilities to the probability distributions their flows can approximate.
method: Quantitatively relate finite-sample point interpolation to Wasserstein approximation.
Derive universality criteria from L^p approximation of transport maps.
Combine one-dimensional Sobolev approximation with shear-type mixing for total variation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical bounds and universality results, not datasets or empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Universality depends on assumptions such as compactly supported, absolutely continuous base measures; coordinate-wise dynamics alone are insufficient for total-variation universality in dimensions d ≥ 2.
infographic.paper_title: Point interpolation and distributional universality in flow-based generative models

title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
authors: Rileigh Bandy, Teresa Portone, Mohammad Khalil, Eric Crislip, Kyle Neal
abstract: Increased computing power has transformed computational science and improved predictive capabilities for complex systems, but many phenomena still exceed current simulation capabilities or require rapid evaluations for fast design iterations. Closure models address this challenge by approximating unresolved effects in reduced or incomplete dynamical systems. Data-driven closures offer a flexible mechanism for improving model accuracy and applicability, but approaches that embed the closure within a computational model for construction and training phases can be computationally expensive and cause numerical instabilities in the computational model during training. To avoid the challenges posed by embedded approaches, staged approaches to closure-model learning have been developed. The first stage uses data assimilation to infer state and closure trajectories from observations. The second stage trains a machine learning closure model offline using the assimilated data, thereby avoiding repeated simulator calls during training. In this work, we investigate the cost and accuracy tradeoffs between embedded and staged data-driven closure modeling approaches for a synthetic epidemiological SIQR model with a nonlinear state-dependent quarantine closure. The results illustrate a practical accuracy-efficiency trade-off: for this exemplar, embedded training provides the strongest average accuracy, while the staged approach yields comparable qualitative behavior with a moderate increase in error, substantially fewer model evaluations, and improved optimization robustness.

infographic.key_insight: Staged closure learning trades moderately higher error for substantially fewer model evaluations and more robust optimization than embedded training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning closures offline from assimilated trajectories can reduce training costs for reduced dynamical models by avoiding repeated simulator calls.
method: Compare embedded closure training with a two-stage data-assimilation approach.
Infer state and closure trajectories from observations, then train a machine learning closure offline.
Evaluate accuracy and computational cost on a synthetic SIQR epidemiological model with a nonlinear, state-dependent quarantine closure.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the synthetic SIQR evaluation, embedded training achieved the best average accuracy, while staged learning preserved comparable qualitative behavior with moderately higher error and substantially fewer model evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: The findings come from one synthetic exemplar, so the accuracy–efficiency trade-off may differ for other systems or observation conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Closure Learning in Dynamical Systems: A Comparison of Data-Assimilated and Embedded Approaches
